title: Seed spirals
topic: Why do seeds grow in spirals?

cards.title: Sunflower head
cards.text: The middle of a sunflower, still green at the centre. Two sets of spirals cross in it, one turning each way, so the first thing to do is count them.

cards.title: Ripe sunflower seeds
cards.text: A head gone to seed, close up. With the florets gone the dark seeds lie like scales, and a row can be followed with a finger from the middle outward.

cards.title: Counting 657 real sunflowers
cards.text: A citizen science study of 657 sunflowers. Most of the spiral counts were Fibonacci numbers, but not all, and on some heads no count could be settled.

cards.title: Pine cone from the stalk
cards.text: A pine cone seen from its stalk end, lying on the ground. The scales wind out from the middle in two directions, the same crossing as in the sunflower.

cards.title: Art Forms in Nature, plate 94: conifers
cards.text: Cones and sprigs of conifers from Haeckel’s book of 1904. He set down each cone scale by scale, and the crossing rows of the pine cone pin are all there.

cards.title: Romanesco with numbered spirals
cards.text: Someone has traced the spirals on a romanesco and numbered them: 13 in black one way, 8 in red the other. Here the counting is already done.

cards.title: Cauliflower with drawn spirals
cards.text: A plain cauliflower with its spirals drawn over, red one way and blue the other. Lumpier than the romanesco, but the same two sets are there.

cards.title: Romanesco, whole
cards.text: The whole head on white, without the lines. Every bud is a small cone made of smaller buds, so the same winding shows again at each size.

cards.title: Spiral aloe
cards.text: Leaves, not seeds: an aloe whose leaves wind round the centre in one sweep. If leaves pack this way too, the spiral is not only a matter of seeds.

cards.title: African Aloe, plate 47
cards.text: An aloe in a blue pot, a colour print from a plant book published in 1736. The leaves climb round the stem in turn, set down long before the photograph in the pin.

cards.title: Rosette of ribbed leaves
cards.text: A rosette seen from straight above. Each leaf lies in the gap between two older ones, and the rows curve both ways out from the bud.

cards.title: Cactus from above
cards.text: A round cactus seen from the top. Each tuft of white spines is one dot, and the dots fall into curving rows that run out from the crown.

cards.title: Cactus crown, close
cards.text: Closer in on another cactus. Near the middle the bumps are small and tight; they widen as they move out, and the spiral rows stay unbroken.

cards.title: Orange florets, close
cards.text: The centre of an orange flower, near enough to see each floret as a bead. Small ones in the middle, larger ones outside, in the same crossing rows.

cards.title: Flower head with red tips
cards.text: A flower head with red-tipped scales round cream ones that wind into a brown centre. Again the parts shrink toward the middle and spiral in.

cards.title: Kiwi slice
cards.text: A kiwi cut across: the seeds sit in a ring round the core, set like spokes. Not every seed pattern is a spiral, so the spiral must have a cause.

cards.title: Golden angle diagram
cards.text: A circle cut into a long arc and a short one in the golden ratio. The short arc spans about 137.5°, the turn between one sunflower floret and the next.

cards.title: A better way to construct the sunflower head
cards.text: Vogel’s model: give each floret the same turn from the one before, and set it a little farther from the centre. Those two rules draw the head.

cards.title: Vogel’s formula, 500 florets
cards.text: Vogel’s formula plotted for florets 1 to 500. Nothing in it mentions a spiral, yet the dots fall into the same crossing rows as the pins.

cards.title: One turn, repeated
cards.text: No seed knows about the spiral. Each new one takes the same turn from the last, the older ones move outward, and the rows appear by themselves.

cards.title: Spirals made in a physics laboratory
cards.text: The same Fibonacci patterns made in a laboratory experiment and in a simulation, with no plant: they arise when new elements appear one after another.

cards.title: Six spirals in one picture
cards.text: A collage: curled leaves, a cut shell, a sunflower, an aloe, a galaxy and a storm. It says they are one shape, so the tree goes to look at the far ones.

cards.title: Storm seen from orbit
cards.text: A storm over the sea from high above, its cloud wound into a tight spiral round a small clear middle. The aloe again, at a very different size.

cards.title: Two cyclones near Iceland
cards.text: Two storms like the one in the pin, seen by NASA’s Terra satellite in November 2006. NASA’s note explains them: a cyclone is low pressure with winds that spiral inwards.

cards.title: Awa Province: Naruto Whirlpools
cards.text: A woodblock print of 1855: the sea between rocks turning into a whirlpool. The storm’s shape in water, drawn long before anyone saw a storm from above.

cards.title: Hurricane Isabel from the space station
cards.text: Hurricane Isabel photographed from the International Space Station on 13 September 2003. From the side it is one flat disc of cloud with the eye as its hub.

cards.title: A storm turns, a seed head does not
cards.text: Storm, whirlpool and galaxy are things in motion, wound up as they turn. A seed head never turns. Its spiral is only the order the seeds were made in.

cards.title: The Sunflower galaxy
cards.text: Messier 63, known as the Sunflower galaxy, in infrared light from NASA’s Spitzer Space Telescope, which picks out its dusty spiral arms. Even the name borrows from the flower.

cards.title: The Shell
cards.text: An etching of one seashell, dated 1650 in the plate. Its spiral shows at the blunt end; the cut shell in the collage shows such a coil from the inside.

cards.title: Seed head on black
cards.text: A white seed head on black, each seed a small star, in crossing spirals round a green centre. It could pass for a drawing of a network.

cards.title: Network drawn as a flower
cards.text: From the Graph board: bright dots on long threads bursting from one point on a stalk. A network drawn the way a seed head is built, out from one centre.

cards.title: Bursts of coloured threads
cards.text: A poster of coloured threads fanning from a few points, each ending in a dot; its own caption calls them neurones. The spread is a seed head’s, the spacing is not.

cards.title: Internet map, 1999
cards.text: A map of the Internet whose caption dates it 18 Feb 1999. Thousands of routes branch outward and fill the page like florets, but nothing spaces them evenly.

cards.title: Bright dots in a dark disc
cards.text: Another from the Graph board: small bright specks and a few larger blots scattered inside one dark circle. A seed head with the rule taken out.

cards.title: Disc packed with small pictures
cards.text: Hundreds of tiny logos and faces crowded into one circle. As full as a flower head but piled at random, which makes the seed head’s order easier to see.

cards.title: Cherry blossom print
cards.text: A branch of pink blossom in flat colour against a blue disc: drawn, not photographed. It turned the tree toward how flowers were set down before cameras.

cards.title: Chrysanthemum and Horsefly
cards.text: A woodblock print from Hokusai’s series of Large Flowers. Each chrysanthemum is built petal by petal in rings round its centre, much as the pin builds its blossom.

cards.title: Sunflowers
cards.text: Two sunflowers in a jug, in pen and watercolour, dated 20 August 1895 on the sheet. The seed discs are dotted in rings: he saw a pattern and did not count it.

cards.title: Fern study, Hatton Fern Album
cards.text: A pressed fern beside its cyanotype, the same frond in white on blue, from about 1850. Here the plant leaves its own outline, with no drawing hand between.

cards.title: Young fern fronds, enlarged
cards.text: Blossfeldt’s photograph of young maidenhair fern fronds, about six times life size, printed in a German photography annual of 1935. The camera looks closer than the pencil did, and finds a coil.

cards.title: Romanesco in black and white
cards.text: A pin that could sit in Blossfeldt’s book: romanesco close up, without colour, lit like a carving. Every bud repeats the whole head.

cards.title: Curled dry leaf
cards.text: One dry leaf curled into a coil on a wooden board. Like the fern fronds it is a spiral made by rolling up, not by packing seeds.

cards.title: Sand patterns made by sound
cards.text: Fifteen squares of pale powder gathered into lines, loops and grids round a centre point, the figures sand makes on a plate that is made to ring. No seed and no growth, and still a pattern.

cards.title: Chladni’s sound figures
cards.text: Thirty figures from Chladni’s Acoustics of 1802: the lines fine powder settles into on a square plate when sound makes it vibrate. The pin’s patterns, drawn by hand.

cards.title: Order without a plan
cards.text: Sand settles where the plate is still; a seed takes the next free place. In both, one simple rule repeated leaves a pattern that nobody drew.
